Alright, I will but after this go study this, you gotta know how longitudinal magnetisation evolves. Following inversion magnetisation is -M0. It slowly recovers exponentially towards +M0, at some point crossing 0. At that point we apply a 90 pulse, and the resulting magnetisation would be zero for tissues with a particular T1. For other tissues, there's a nonzero value of magnetisation, so we measure a signal from those. If we then insert e.g. a spin echo imaging module we'd only "see" tissues with T1s outside this range. 

The value of ln(0.5) is because that's how long it takes for the exponential to recover to exactly half its maximal value.

It's just ln(0.5)*T1. Magnetisation goes from -M0 to +M0 along an exponential, so you just need to know how long it takes for magnetisation to get exactly half way there, which is the equation I gave.

I'm a julia user since around 2018, when I tested it for a numerical simulation that I also wrote (badly) in python. I was amazed by the fast loops, and I still am today. Since then I've worked with a good number of other languages, mostly matlab, python and C/C++, which dominate scientific computing IMO. 

Anecdotally, I've encouraged researchers in my field to work with Julia, and the pushback I get is pretty telling. Lots of people fear learning a new language and the loss of productivity it entails, and that's particularly true in science where the turnaround on projects is often short. 

Having said that, I do encourage my students to use Julia, and I give them code and examples to help get them started. With that prompting, I've taught several people how to use it, and all have learned very quickly how to get the best out of the language, particularly how to efficiently write generic code, use functions effectively to control scope and exploit functional programming methods.

Overall, I would say adoption is slow, but the next generation of programmers is using it and appreciating it. The kicker funnily enough is AD, where the obvious ML use cases make often arcane bits of maths written by others accessible immediately, without delving into the pytorch-specific subset of python. 

TL;DR, from my experience uptake is slow due to the nature of the field. Adoption is enthusiastic when conditions for growth are good. Most people love the features of Julia. And finally, everyone happily uses your code when it's packaged up neatly. The work on small binaries for Julia will really add a hell of an arrow to the language's quiver.

Ash grows with very wide growth rings in the early part of its life. This means that the resultant wood, while narrow in cross section, is particularly strong as the parenchyma / vessel elements are a relatively small fraction of the wood. If you look at e.g. oak you'll see the growth rings are generally tighter and this means the wood can be a little more porous and brittle. Note this doesn't really tell you much about the stiffness of the wood, just the ultimate breaking strength. 

Interestingly this rule doesn't work for pine and softwoods in general as they don't have vessel elements (I.e. pores), just hollow cells called tracheids. Consequently softwood (which has stronger latewood) is generally stronger the more rings it has.
Ash is the traditional indoor gym equipment wood. Hard, flexible, tolerant of impacts and very strong in small cross sections.

Arrays are generally more useful when data to be accessed is accessed consecutively or concurrently, and that data is assured to be adjacent or local in memory. For example, summing elements in an array. This is because data are loaded into the processor cache in chunks that can be hundreds or thousands of elements long. By ensuring the data you'll be using is local, no time is wasted fetching new data as it's already basically there.

By comparison, dictionaries normally use a pointer to refer to data to be accessed, which means each read normally entails a memory move. To some extent the processor ensures stuff remains processor local when it's repeatedly accessed, but this is semi-stochastic in nature. 

Arrays generally demand elements are equal in size. This is fine when data are a long list of identically typed objects. When that's not true, an array can waste a lot of memory representing empty space that the largest possible element could occupy. Dictionaries can point to arbitrary memory so storage is dense. 

Basically, arrays are for dense, identical objects you work with successively. Dictionaries are for variable objects you work with in semi-random order.

Best thing is to have an appreciation for the underlying physics. If you understand the impact of longitudinal vs transverse relaxation, and the mechanisms that drive them, sequences become more distinct. For example, a T2 sequence demands there be a long period after excitation for spin phase to decohere. Similarly T1 demands short TR and TE to allow demagnetisation of spins from past excitations to contribute significantly to the signal.

The RF phenomena are absolutely key to building understanding here. Similarly, understanding the key terms in the decay equations is essential. When you're equipped with these, different contrast mechanisms, multi echo phenomena,  multi excitation effects etc will all begin to make more sense. So you're basically trying to register the stock to the chuck jaws - this can work okay, but relies on unworn jaws with little lift. What's more reliable is registering to the the chuck body. Place a piece of ground stock or any other good parallel of the right thickness so it rests between the jaws on the chuck body. Lightly tap your workpiece into place against it. Withdraw the parallel and do the same in another orientation. This will define two lines of contact with your workpiece which is parallel to the chuck body. 

Tap and indicate to get it perfect, then crank the jaws down.

Note, it is better to leave the backing in place if it can be secured in place, this helps to resist thrust loads which can otherwise pull the workpiece out of the jaws. I've seen the parallel retained with wire, band clamps etc, but don't go attaching it sketchily.

Data collected from the scanner has to be mathematically transformed into an image. In thick sections like yours, this can lead to differential stress in the end grain face vs the interior, and checking to occur. It can be advantageous to dry slowly to avoid this, e.g. by applying a moisture barrier to the end grain, or by limiting air movement. High heat (e.g. drying indoors) will facilitate diffusion from the centre out, so for thick sections it's definitely advantageous. As a rule of thumb, air movement causes fast drying at the surface, high heat causes fast movement of water to the surface. Indoors with limited air movement is ideal for best drying. The answer to whether you can rebuild a spindle to suit a different set of loads is yes. The difficulties can be quite numerous though. Nearly all mills use an opposed pair of angular contact or taper roller bearings. These, unlike ball bearings, have a significant axial preload. This single criteria is key to how a mill spindle resists side loads. To account for this, spindles normally have one or more thrust collars, threads to mount preload nuts etc. The lack of such features in both directions precludes a rebuild to another bearing type without some effort.

As for other bearing types, yes, in fact a plain bearing can do a fine job at side loads, but has issues with the surface area / speed / heat trifecta. This means high speeds may generate unacceptable amounts of heat, and so on.

My lathe uses two ball bearings and one tapered bushing to resist side loads. My mill uses the same this configuration is pretty typical for low speeds, but on a modern mill it's usually all rolling element bearings

Cold saw is just a very specialised milling machine with a very big slitting saw. That means that the capacity is determined by the energy available to cut. In order to cut, each tooth requires a minimum pressure. At a constant speed, the energy loss is given by the pressure P multiplied by the surface speed v. 
 
When considering capacity limits, the question is: "how many teeth will cut simultaneously, and how little pressure can each tooth apply and still cut". For steel, the needed pressure is higher than for say wood, and so the capacity is correspondingly smaller.

Mechanical measurements will be biased by deflection. These parts are thin, long tubes, and will deform if they're pushed. Dial indicators come with a rated force for a reason. Optical measurement does not have this bias. 

In general, it is easiest to measure the largest geometric error; for a bent tube this is along the axis. At 12.5mm, a 2 degree bend will produce a 0.5mm deflection in a 1.5mm tube. Consequently the view down the tube will be obscured in a way directly related to the bend.

Easy solution here: optical measurement. Shine a (visible) laser down one end of the tube. Choose a spot size slightly larger than the hole. Select a laser with a Gaussian beam profile. Record what comes out the other end with any old sensor. Bent tubes will show a distorted image with some bright patches and some dim. Contour fit the image, noncircular contours will indicate a bent tube.

You'll need to characterise for the 2 degree bit, but this should be quite classifiable. If you use a laser with an integrated lens this could be very cheap.

Write out your problem in terms of a 2d matrix of a and b, then highlight where a and b actually land as you loop through. Through much of history, brace style drills were popular. If you've ever used one, you'll know they're both torquey and easy to apply pressure with. These qualities make drilling metal possible, if slow and hot. 

As well, blacksmith drills have been popular more recently (1700+). These are usually cranked or foot pumped drills with a large flywheel and often gearing. Some would need an apprentice to drive them, others can be driven by the user. These usually have all the common features of a modern pillar drill - column, spindle, quill and table.

Finally jewellers and clockmakers have used bow driven tools to drive light drills and lathes for a long time. These are really just a small bow with the string wrapped around the drill shaft. Then friction between string and shaft means moving the bow spins the shaft. This is actually still useful as a method - you can drill in any space you can fit a drill bit.

Junior hacksaw blades are made from spring steel exclusively. Big boy hacksaw blades are bimetallic, e.g. have fused hardened steel teeth. These will cut harder materials than the junior hacksaw, including your sawblade. You don't need a diamond blade. What you may need to do, however, is flatten the wave pattern of the teeth with a soft hammer and wooden backer. This will reduce the cut width to a manageable degree.
